title: Rearrange K Substrings to Form Target String
statement:
The strings `s` and `t` are anagrams of each other (they contain the same letters, each the same number of times), and the integer `k` divides their common length.

Cut `s` into `k` consecutive pieces, all of length `s.length / k`. Return `true` if those pieces can be placed in some order so that joining them gives exactly `t`, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: s and t contain only lowercase English letters
s and t are anagrams of each other
signature: boolean isPossibleToRearrange(String s, String t, int k)
notes:
## Intuition

Moving pieces around never changes the pieces themselves. If the pieces of `s` can be joined into `t`, then cutting `t` every `s.length / k` characters gives back exactly those pieces, in their new order. So the answer is `true` exactly when the pieces of `s` and the pieces of `t` are the same strings, each appearing the same number of times. Trying all `k!` orders would work but is hopeless; counting the pieces in a hash map compares the two collections in linear time.

## Approach

1. Let `size = s.length / k`, the length of every piece.
2. Cut `s` every `size` characters and add one to `count` for each `piece`.
3. Cut `t` the same way. For each `piece`, read `left`, the number of unused copies of it that `s` still has.
4. If `left` is `0`, `t` needs a piece that `s` cannot supply: return `false`. Otherwise use up one copy.
5. Both strings have `k` pieces, so if every piece of `t` found a partner, they match one to one: return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "abcd"`, `t = "cdab"`, `k = 2`, so `size = 2`. The pieces of `s` are `"ab"` and `"cd"`, giving `count = {ab: 1, cd: 1}`. The first piece of `t` is `"cd"`: `left = 1`, so it is used and `cd` drops to `0`. The second is `"ab"`: `left = 1`, so `ab` drops to `0`. Every piece matched, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n), where n is `s.length`: each character is copied into one piece and each piece is hashed a constant number of times.
- Space: O(n) for the pieces stored in `count`.

## Pitfalls

- Comparing the sets of distinct pieces is not enough. `s = "ababba"` and `t = "abbaba"` with `k = 3` both use only `"ab"` and `"ba"`, but `s` has two `"ab"` and `t` has two `"ba"`, so the answer is `false`.
- Being anagrams does not make the answer `true`: with `k = 1` the only piece is `s` itself, so it must equal `t`.
- Cut `t` at the same multiples of `size` as `s`; any other split of `t` says nothing about how the pieces line up.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `size` | the length of each piece, `s.length / k` |
| `count` | for each piece of `s`, how many copies are not yet matched |
| `start` | the index where the current piece begins |
| `piece` | the current piece of `s` or `t` |
| `left` | unmatched copies in `s` of the current piece of `t` |

narration.2: Every one of the k pieces has this length, because k divides the length of s.
narration.3: count maps each piece of s to how many of its copies are still unmatched.
narration.5: Step through s one piece at a time.
narration.6: Cut out the piece that starts at index start.
narration.7: Count one more copy of this piece.
narration.10: Cut t at the same places: in any rearrangement, each piece occupies one of these slots.
narration.11: Take the piece of t that fills this slot.
narration.12: How many unmatched copies of it does s still have?
narration.13: None left: t needs a piece that s cannot supply...
narration.14: ...so no order of the pieces can produce t.
narration.16: Use up one copy for this slot.
narration.18: All k slots of t were filled by the k pieces of s, so a valid order exists.
